title: Statistics
description: Free Statistics study guide: 8 units covering data displays, the normal curve, correlation, study design, probability, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. 96 practice questions with explanations, 64 flashcards and a practice exam.

units.name: Describing Data & Graphs

concepts.intro: Every analysis starts by asking what kind of variable you have, because that decides which graphs and summaries make sense.
b: Categorical (qualitative) variables place individuals into groups: eye color, favorite sport, yes/no answers
Quantitative variables are numbers where arithmetic makes sense: height, test score, minutes of sleep
A number can still be categorical: zip codes and jersey numbers are labels, so averaging them is meaningless
Categorical data → bar charts and pie charts; quantitative data → dotplots, stemplots, histograms and boxplots
Always identify the individuals (who or what is measured) and the variables (what is recorded about each)

concepts.intro: To describe a quantitative distribution, cover Shape, Outliers, Center and Spread, always in context.
b: Shape: symmetric, skewed right (long tail toward large values), skewed left (long tail toward small values); unimodal or bimodal
Outliers: values that fall far from the rest; the 1.5 × IQR rule flags points below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR
Center: the mean (balance point) or median (middle value)
Spread: range, interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1) or standard deviation
Always name the variable and units, e.g. 'the median commute is 22 minutes', not just 'the median is 22'

concepts.intro: Some summaries barely move when an extreme value appears; others get dragged toward it.
b: The median and IQR are resistant: an outlier has little effect on them
The mean, standard deviation and range are not resistant: one extreme value can move them a lot
In a right-skewed distribution the mean is usually greater than the median; in a left-skewed one it is usually less
For skewed data or data with outliers, report median and IQR; for roughly symmetric data, mean and standard deviation
The five-number summary (min, Q1, median, Q3, max) is what a boxplot draws

keyFacts: Mean > median usually signals right skew; mean < median usually signals left skew.
IQR = Q3 − Q1 measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
Outlier fences: Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR.
Standard deviation is roughly the typical distance of values from the mean.
traps: A histogram of quantitative data has touching bars; a bar chart of categories has gaps. Don't mix them up.
'Skewed right' means the tail points right (toward larger values), not that most data is on the right.
A large standard deviation doesn't mean the data is 'wrong'. It just means the values are spread out.

units.name: Distributions & Normal Curve

concepts.l: Density Curves and the Normal Model
concepts.intro: A normal curve is a smooth, symmetric, bell-shaped model described completely by its mean μ and standard deviation σ.
b: The total area under any density curve is 1, and area over an interval is the proportion of values in it
A normal curve is symmetric about μ; the mean, median and mode are all equal
σ controls the width: a larger σ gives a flatter, wider curve
The inflection points of the curve sit one standard deviation from the mean
Many measurements are approximately normal (heights, measurement error), but not all. Check with a graph first

concepts.intro: In a normal distribution, fixed percentages of the data fall within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.
b: About 68% of values fall within μ ± 1σ
About 95% fall within μ ± 2σ
About 99.7% fall within μ ± 3σ
By symmetry, about 16% lie above μ + 1σ and about 2.5% lie above μ + 2σ
The rule only applies to distributions that are approximately normal

concepts.intro: A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, which lets you compare values from different distributions.
b: z = (x − μ) / σ; positive z is above the mean, negative z is below
A z-score of 2 means the value is two standard deviations above average
The pth percentile is the value with p% of the data at or below it
For normal data, a z-table or calculator (normalcdf) converts z-scores to proportions
Comparing z-scores shows which result is more unusual relative to its own group

keyFacts: 68–95–99.7: the percent of normal data within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.
z = (x − μ)/σ measures position in standard deviations.
z = 0 is the mean; about 84% of normal data lies below z = 1.
The area under a density curve is always exactly 1.
traps: Don't apply the empirical rule to skewed data. It only works for approximately normal distributions.
A negative z-score isn't 'bad'. It only means the value is below the mean.
Percentile is not percent correct: scoring at the 90th percentile means beating about 90% of others.

units.name: Correlation vs Causation

concepts.intro: A scatterplot shows the relationship between two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals.
b: Put the explanatory variable on the x-axis and the response variable on the y-axis
Describe direction (positive/negative), form (linear/curved), strength and unusual points
Positive association: as x increases, y tends to increase; negative: y tends to decrease
An outlier in a scatterplot falls outside the overall pattern
An influential point is one whose removal would noticeably change the line or correlation

concepts.intro: r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship on a scale from −1 to 1.
b: r near +1 or −1 means a strong linear relationship; r near 0 means a weak linear relationship
r has no units and doesn't change if you swap x and y or change units of measurement
r only measures linear association: a perfect curve can have r close to 0
r is not resistant: a single outlier can greatly change it
r² (coefficient of determination) is the fraction of variation in y explained by the linear model with x

concepts.intro: Two variables can move together without one causing the other.
b: A confounding (lurking) variable can drive both: ice cream sales and drownings both rise with summer heat
The direction could be reversed: does exercise improve mood, or do happier people exercise more?
Coincidence: with enough variables, some will correlate by chance
Only a well-designed randomized experiment can establish cause and effect
Observational studies can show association and motivate experiments, but can't prove causation

keyFacts: −1 ≤ r ≤ 1; the sign gives direction, the magnitude gives strength of the linear relationship.
r² = proportion of variation in y explained by the regression on x.
Correlation doesn't imply causation; confounding variables are the usual culprit.
Least-squares regression line: ŷ = a + bx, passing through (x̄, ȳ).
traps: r = 0 doesn't mean 'no relationship'. It means no linear relationship; there could be a strong curve.
A strong correlation between two variables doesn't mean one causes the other.
Don't extrapolate: predictions far outside the range of x-values in the data are unreliable.

units.name: Sampling & Study Design

concepts.intro: We study a sample to learn about a population, which only works if the sample represents it.
b: Population: the entire group we want information about; sample: the part we actually examine
A parameter describes a population (μ, p); a statistic describes a sample (x̄, p̂)
Bias is a systematic tendency to over- or under-estimate the truth, and bigger samples don't fix it
Voluntary response samples (online polls, call-ins) overrepresent people with strong opinions
Convenience samples (whoever is easy to reach) usually aren't representative

concepts.intro: Chance-based sampling methods avoid favoritism and let us quantify uncertainty.
b: Simple random sample (SRS): every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen
Stratified random sample: split the population into similar groups (strata) and take an SRS from each
Cluster sample: split into groups (clusters), randomly select whole clusters, and survey everyone in them
Systematic sample: pick a random start, then every kth individual
Undercoverage, nonresponse and wording of questions can still bias results even with random selection

concepts.intro: In an experiment the researcher imposes a treatment; in an observational study they only watch.
b: Experiments use random assignment to create comparable groups, which allows cause-and-effect conclusions
Principles of experimental design: comparison, random assignment, control of other variables, replication
A placebo is a fake treatment; blinding keeps subjects (single-blind) or also evaluators (double-blind) unaware of groups
A block design groups similar subjects first, then randomizes treatments within each block
Random sampling lets you generalize to the population; random assignment lets you infer causation

keyFacts: Random sampling → generalize to the population. Random assignment → conclude cause and effect.
Parameters describe populations (μ, p); statistics describe samples (x̄, p̂).
Larger samples reduce variability but do not reduce bias.
Double-blind: neither subjects nor those measuring outcomes know who got which treatment.
traps: Stratified and cluster sampling are different: stratified samples from every group, cluster samples a few whole groups.
An observational study with a huge sample still can't prove causation.
Random assignment and random sampling aren't the same thing. They answer different questions.

units.name: Probability Basics

concepts.intro: Probability is the long-run relative frequency of an outcome over many repetitions of a chance process.
b: Probabilities are between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain)
The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes; all their probabilities add to 1
Law of large numbers: as trials increase, the proportion of an outcome approaches its true probability
Short runs can look streaky; the 'gambler's fallacy' wrongly expects chance to self-correct in the short term
Simulation estimates probabilities by imitating a chance process many times

concepts.intro: A few rules combine the probabilities of events.
b: Complement rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
Mutually exclusive events can't both happen, so P(A and B) = 0
Multiplication rule for independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) · P(B)
'At least one' problems are easiest with the complement: 1 − P(none)

concepts.intro: Conditional probability updates the chance of an event once we know another event occurred.
b: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), read 'probability of A given B'
Events are independent if knowing one occurred doesn't change the probability of the other: P(A | B) = P(A)
Two-way tables make conditional probabilities concrete: restrict to the row or column you're given
Tree diagrams organize multi-stage processes; multiply along branches, add across branches
Mutually exclusive events with nonzero probabilities are never independent

keyFacts: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Independent: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A).
P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
traps: Don't add probabilities of events that can happen together without subtracting the overlap.
Mutually exclusive isn't the same as independent. Disjoint events are dependent.
P(A | B) is usually not equal to P(B | A).

units.name: Confidence Intervals

concepts.intro: A statistic varies from sample to sample; its sampling distribution describes that variation.
b: The sampling distribution of x̄ is centered at μ: the sample mean is an unbiased estimator
Its standard deviation is σ/√n, so quadrupling n cuts the variability in half
Central Limit Theorem: for large n (often n ≥ 30), the distribution of x̄ is approximately normal regardless of the population's shape
For proportions, p̂ is centered at p with standard deviation √(p(1−p)/n)
Variability of a statistic depends on sample size, not on population size (as long as the population is much larger)

concepts.intro: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a parameter: estimate ± margin of error.
b: General form: statistic ± (critical value)(standard error)
For a proportion: p̂ ± z*·√(p̂(1−p̂)/n); z* = 1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%
For a mean with unknown σ: x̄ ± t*·s/√n, using the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
Conditions: random sample, independence (n ≤ 10% of population), and normality/large counts
Large counts for proportions: n·p̂ ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10

concepts.intro: The confidence level describes the method, not any single interval.
b: Interpret an interval: 'We are 95% confident the interval from __ to __ captures the true [parameter in context]'
Confidence level: if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals would capture the parameter
Higher confidence → wider interval; larger sample size → narrower interval
The margin of error covers only random sampling error, not bias from poor sampling or wording
It's wrong to say there is a 95% probability the parameter is in this specific interval: the parameter is fixed

keyFacts: Standard deviation of x̄ = σ/√n; of p̂ = √(p(1−p)/n).
95% confidence uses z* = 1.96.
Margin of error shrinks as n grows (by a factor of 1/√n) and grows with confidence level.
CLT: x̄ is approximately normal for large n, whatever the population's shape.
traps: A 95% confidence interval doesn't contain 95% of the data values. It estimates a parameter.
The margin of error doesn't account for bias.
Doubling the sample size doesn't halve the margin of error. You need four times the sample.

units.name: Hypothesis Testing Logic

concepts.l: Hypotheses and the Logic of a Test
concepts.intro: A significance test asks whether sample evidence is strong enough to reject a claim about a parameter.
b: Null hypothesis H₀: the 'no effect' or status-quo claim, e.g. p = 0.5
Alternative hypothesis Hₐ: what we suspect is true instead, e.g. p > 0.5 (one-sided) or p ≠ 0.5 (two-sided)
Hypotheses are always about parameters (p, μ), never about sample statistics
We assume H₀ is true and ask how surprising our sample result would be
Test statistic: (statistic − null value) / standard error

concepts.intro: The P-value measures how surprising the data are if the null hypothesis is true.
b: P-value: the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed
Small P-value → the data would be unusual if H₀ were true → evidence against H₀
Compare with the significance level α (often 0.05): if P ≤ α, reject H₀; otherwise fail to reject H₀
Failing to reject H₀ doesn't prove H₀ is true; there just isn't convincing evidence against it
Always state the conclusion in context: 'There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of...'

concepts.intro: Every decision can be wrong, and the two kinds of mistakes have different consequences.
b: Type I error: rejecting H₀ when it's actually true (a false alarm); P(Type I) = α
Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when Hₐ is true (a missed effect)
Power = P(rejecting H₀ when Hₐ is true) = 1 − P(Type II)
Power increases with larger sample size, larger α, and a larger true effect
Statistical significance isn't practical importance: a tiny effect can be 'significant' with a huge sample

keyFacts: P-value = P(result at least this extreme | H₀ true).
Reject H₀ when P-value ≤ α.
Type I = false positive (probability α); Type II = false negative.
Power = 1 − P(Type II error); bigger n means more power.
traps: The P-value is not the probability that H₀ is true.
Never 'accept H₀'. You either reject it or fail to reject it.
Hypotheses use parameters (p, μ), not statistics (p̂, x̄).

units.name: Misleading Statistics in the Wild

concepts.intro: A graph can be accurate in its numbers and still leave a false impression.
b: Truncated y-axis: starting the axis above 0 makes small differences look huge in bar charts
Inconsistent scales or uneven time intervals distort trends
Pictographs that scale an image in two dimensions exaggerate differences (double the height → four times the area)
3-D and pie charts with many slices make comparisons hard to judge
Cherry-picked time windows can make a trend appear or disappear

concepts.intro: The same data can be summarized in ways that inflate or hide an effect.
b: Relative vs. absolute risk: a risk rising from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 is a '100% increase' but only 1 extra case per 10,000
Averages can mislead with skewed data: the mean income of a room changes a lot when a billionaire walks in
Percent vs. percentage points: going from 10% to 15% is a 5-percentage-point rise, but a 50% increase
Survivorship bias: studying only the successes (e.g. companies still in business) hides the failures
Base rates matter: a 99%-accurate test for a rare condition still produces many false positives

concepts.l: Simpson's Paradox and Reading Claims Critically
concepts.intro: A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined.
b: Simpson's paradox happens when a lurking variable is unevenly distributed across groups
Classic example: a treatment can have a higher success rate in each hospital separately but a lower rate overall
Ask who was studied, how they were chosen, and what was compared
Check whether the study was an experiment or observational before accepting a causal claim
Look for sample size, margin of error and whether the source has a stake in the result

keyFacts: Truncated axes exaggerate differences in bar charts.
Relative risk sounds bigger than absolute risk. Ask for both.
A change from 10% to 15% is 5 percentage points but a 50% relative increase.
Simpson's paradox: a lurking variable can reverse a trend when groups are combined.
traps: Don't judge a bar chart by bar heights alone. Check where the y-axis starts.
'Doubles your risk' can still mean a very small absolute risk.
An impressive statistic from a biased sample is still biased.

quiz.q: Which of these is a categorical variable?
quiz.e: Zip codes are labels. Averaging them has no meaning, so they are categorical even though they are numbers.

quiz.q: A distribution has a long tail stretching toward larger values. It is:
quiz.e: Skew is named for the direction of the tail. A tail toward large values is right (positive) skew.

quiz.q: In a strongly right-skewed distribution of incomes, which is most likely true?
o: The mean is greater than the median
The mean is less than the median
The median is pulled toward the tail
quiz.e: The few very large incomes pull the mean up; the median, a resistant measure, stays near the bulk of the data.

quiz.q: Which measure of center is resistant to outliers?
quiz.e: The median depends only on the middle position, so extreme values barely change it.

quiz.q: A data set has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 30. Which value would be flagged as an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule?
quiz.e: IQR = 10, so the fences are 20 − 15 = 5 and 30 + 15 = 45. Only 46 falls outside.

quiz.q: What does a boxplot display?
quiz.e: A boxplot draws min, Q1, median, Q3 and max (with outliers often plotted separately).

quiz.q: Which graph is appropriate for showing the distribution of favorite music genres in a class?
quiz.e: Music genre is categorical, so a bar chart (or pie chart) is appropriate.

quiz.q: Adding 10 points to every student's test score changes which statistic?
quiz.e: Shifting every value by a constant moves measures of center but leaves all measures of spread unchanged.

quiz.q: Multiplying every value in a data set by 3 does what to the standard deviation?
quiz.e: Rescaling by a factor multiplies measures of spread by that factor. The variance would be multiplied by 9.

quiz.q: The data 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8 has what median?
quiz.e: With six values, the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (4 + 5)/2 = 4.5.

quiz.q: Which summary pair is best for a distribution with a clear outlier?
quiz.e: Median and IQR are both resistant, so the outlier doesn't distort them.

quiz.q: A standard deviation of 0 means:
o: Every value in the data set is identical
There are no outliers but values differ
quiz.e: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. It is 0 only if every value equals the mean.

quiz.q: SAT Math scores are roughly normal with mean 520 and SD 110. About what percent of scores fall between 410 and 630?
quiz.e: 410 and 630 are one SD below and above the mean, so about 68% by the empirical rule.

quiz.q: Using the same distribution (mean 520, SD 110), about what percent of scores are above 740?
quiz.e: 740 is 2 SD above the mean. 95% lie within ±2 SD, leaving 5% in both tails, so 2.5% above.

quiz.q: A test has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of a score of 58?
Ana scores 85 on a test with mean 75 and SD 5. Ben scores 90 on a test with mean 80 and SD 10. Who did better relative to their class?
quiz.e: Ana's z = (85−75)/5 = 2; Ben's z = (90−80)/10 = 1. Ana is further above her class average.

quiz.q: What is the total area under a normal density curve?
quiz.e: Every density curve has total area 1, representing 100% of the observations.

quiz.q: Which statement about a normal distribution is true?
o: Mean, median and mode are equal
About 50% of data is within 1 SD of the mean
quiz.e: The normal curve is symmetric and unimodal, so all three centers coincide.

quiz.q: Increasing σ while keeping μ fixed makes the normal curve:
quiz.e: More spread means the same total area of 1 is spread over a wider range, so the peak drops.

quiz.q: A value with z = 0 is:
quiz.e: z measures distance from the mean in SDs; z = 0 means no distance.

quiz.q: About what percent of a normal distribution lies below z = −1?
quiz.e: 68% lies between −1 and 1, leaving 32% in the tails, so 16% below −1.

quiz.q: A student at the 75th percentile of height is:
o: Taller than about 75% of the group
quiz.e: A percentile tells the percent of values at or below that value.

quiz.q: For a normal distribution with mean 100 and SD 15, which value is two standard deviations below the mean?
When is the empirical rule appropriate?
o: When the distribution is approximately normal
quiz.e: The 68–95–99.7 percentages are properties of the normal curve specifically.

quiz.q: Which value of r shows the strongest linear relationship?
quiz.e: Strength depends on the absolute value; |−0.92| is the largest.

quiz.q: Cities with more firefighters report more fire damage. The most likely explanation is:
o: A confounding variable: bigger fires call for more firefighters
The correlation must be a calculation error
Fire damage causes cities to hire firefighters years later
quiz.e: Fire size affects both the number of firefighters sent and the damage, so it is a lurking variable.

quiz.q: A scatterplot shows a perfect U-shaped curve. The correlation r is most likely:
quiz.e: r measures only linear association; a symmetric U shape has no overall linear trend.

quiz.q: If r = 0.8 for height (cm) vs. weight (kg), what is r if height is converted to inches?
quiz.e: r has no units and is unchanged by linear changes of units.

quiz.q: r² = 0.64 for a regression of exam score on hours studied means:
o: Each hour raises the score by 64%
64% of the variation in exam scores is explained by the linear relationship with hours studied
quiz.e: r² is the proportion of variation in the response explained by the model (here r = ±0.8).

quiz.q: Which study design can establish that a new study app causes higher test scores?
o: An observational study of top students
A scatterplot of usage vs. scores
quiz.e: Only random assignment of treatments balances confounding variables so a causal conclusion is justified.

quiz.q: A regression line predicts plant height from days of growth using data from days 1–30. Predicting height at day 200 is an example of:
quiz.e: Predicting far outside the observed x-range is extrapolation, which is unreliable.

quiz.q: The residual for a point is:
quiz.e: Residual = observed − predicted. Positive residuals are above the line.

quiz.q: The explanatory variable belongs on which axis of a scatterplot?
o: Neither; it is shown by color
quiz.e: Convention places the explanatory (predictor) variable on the horizontal axis.

quiz.q: Which is true about the correlation r?
o: It has the units of y
It is not resistant to outliers
It changes if x and y are swapped
quiz.e: A single outlier can pull r strongly toward or away from 0.

quiz.q: In ŷ = 12 + 3x, what does the slope 3 mean?
o: For each 1-unit increase in x, predicted y increases by 3
quiz.e: The slope is the predicted change in y per one-unit increase in x.

quiz.q: The least-squares regression line always passes through:
quiz.e: A property of least-squares regression: the line goes through the point of means.

quiz.q: A TV station asks viewers to text their opinion on a new law. This is a:
quiz.e: People choose whether to respond, so those with strong opinions are overrepresented.

quiz.q: A school divides students by grade and randomly selects 25 students from each grade. This is a:
quiz.e: Each grade is a stratum, and an SRS is taken within every stratum.

quiz.q: A researcher randomly selects 5 homerooms and surveys every student in them. This is a:
quiz.e: Whole groups (clusters) are selected at random and everyone in them is surveyed.

quiz.q: Which conclusion requires random assignment?
o: That results generalize to a population
That a treatment causes an effect
quiz.e: Random assignment balances confounding variables between groups, supporting causal claims.

quiz.q: The average height of all U.S. adults is a:
quiz.e: It describes the whole population, so it is a parameter (usually unknown).

quiz.q: Increasing the sample size of a biased sampling method will:
o: Turn it into a random sample
quiz.e: Bias is systematic. More data from a flawed method gives a more precise wrong answer.

quiz.q: In a drug trial, neither the patients nor the doctors assessing them know who got the real drug. This is:
quiz.e: Blinding both subjects and evaluators is a double-blind design.

quiz.q: Researchers compare heart disease rates of people who already drink coffee and people who don't. This is:
quiz.e: No treatment is imposed; the researchers only observe existing groups.

quiz.q: Why do experiments include a control group?
o: To provide a baseline for comparison
To eliminate the need for random assignment
quiz.e: Comparison with a control shows what happens without the treatment.

quiz.q: A survey question reads, 'Don't you agree that the unfair homework policy should end?' This introduces:
quiz.e: Leading wording pushes respondents toward an answer.

quiz.q: A telephone survey that only calls landlines is likely to suffer from:
quiz.e: People without landlines (many younger adults) can't be selected, so part of the population is left out.

quiz.q: In a block design comparing two fertilizers, fields are first grouped by soil type. The purpose is to:
o: Reduce variability from a known source
quiz.e: Blocking compares treatments within similar units, removing soil-type variation from the comparison.

quiz.q: A fair die is rolled. What is P(not a 6)?
quiz.e: Complement rule: 1 − 1/6 = 5/6.

quiz.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. What is P(A or B)?
A fair coin is flipped twice. What is the probability of two heads?
quiz.e: The flips are independent: (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4.

quiz.q: A fair coin lands heads 5 times in a row. The probability of heads on the next flip is:
quiz.e: Flips are independent; believing tails is due is the gambler's fallacy.

quiz.q: A basketball player makes 70% of free throws, independently. What is P(missing both of two shots)?
Using the same player (70%), what is P(making at least one of two shots)?
In a class, 12 of 30 students play a sport, and 8 of those 12 are seniors. What is P(senior | plays a sport)?
quiz.e: Given 'plays a sport', restrict to those 12 students: 8 of them are seniors.

quiz.q: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?
quiz.e: Mutually exclusive events can't occur together.

quiz.q: If P(A | B) = P(A), then A and B are:
quiz.e: Knowing B occurred doesn't change the probability of A, which is the definition of independence.

quiz.q: The law of large numbers says:
o: The proportion of an outcome approaches its probability as trials increase
Short runs always match the true probability
Outcomes balance out after a streak
quiz.e: Only in the long run does the relative frequency settle near the true probability.

quiz.q: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is P(heart or king)?
quiz.e: 13 hearts + 4 kings − 1 king of hearts = 16 cards.

quiz.q: Which describes independent events?
o: Being a senior and being a freshman
Rain today and a wet sidewalk today
Rolling a 3 on one die and a 5 on another
quiz.e: Separate dice don't affect each other; the other pairs are dependent or mutually exclusive.

quiz.q: A poll of 400 randomly chosen voters finds p̂ = 0.55. What is the approximate 95% margin of error?
Which change makes a confidence interval narrower?
quiz.e: Standard error shrinks with larger n, so the margin of error shrinks.

quiz.q: To cut the margin of error in half, you should:
quiz.e: Margin of error is proportional to 1/√n, so halving it requires 4 times the sample.

quiz.q: A 95% confidence interval for mean sleep is (6.8, 7.4) hours. The correct interpretation is:
o: 95% of students sleep between 6.8 and 7.4 hours
There is a 95% chance the sample mean is in the interval
We are 95% confident the interval from 6.8 to 7.4 hours captures the true mean sleep time
The true mean is definitely 7.1 hours
quiz.e: The interval estimates the population mean, and the 95% describes the method's long-run capture rate.

quiz.q: What does '95% confidence' refer to?
o: 95% of the data lies in the interval
The parameter changes 95% of the time
About 95% of intervals from repeated samples would capture the parameter
quiz.e: Confidence is a property of the procedure over many samples.

quiz.q: The Central Limit Theorem says the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately normal when:
quiz.e: For large n, x̄ is approximately normal regardless of the population shape.

quiz.q: The standard deviation of x̄ for samples of size 25 from a population with σ = 10 is:
Which critical value is used for a 99% confidence interval for a proportion?
quiz.e: 99% leaves 0.5% in each tail, which corresponds to z* ≈ 2.576.

quiz.q: An interval for a proportion requires n·p̂ ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10. This condition checks that:
o: The sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately normal
quiz.e: Large counts make the normal approximation to the sampling distribution reasonable.

quiz.q: A survey of gym members about exercise habits reports a margin of error of ±3%. This margin accounts for:
o: Bias from surveying only gym members
quiz.e: Margin of error measures chance variation, not systematic bias.

quiz.q: Why do we use t* instead of z* for a mean when σ is unknown?
o: Estimating σ with s adds uncertainty, and the t distribution accounts for it
quiz.e: The t distribution has heavier tails to reflect the extra uncertainty from using s.

quiz.q: A 90% and a 99% interval are built from the same sample. Which is wider?
quiz.e: Higher confidence requires a larger critical value, so the interval is wider.

quiz.q: A company claims 40% of customers prefer its brand. A researcher suspects it's less. The correct hypotheses are:
quiz.e: Hypotheses concern the parameter p, and the suspicion 'less' makes a one-sided alternative.

quiz.q: A P-value of 0.02 means:
o: There is a 2% chance H₀ is true
If H₀ were true, there would be a 2% chance of results at least as extreme as observed
There is a 98% chance Hₐ is true
quiz.e: The P-value is computed assuming H₀ is true; it is not the probability H₀ is true.

quiz.q: With α = 0.05 and P-value = 0.08, you should:
quiz.e: 0.08 > 0.05, so the evidence isn't strong enough to reject H₀.

quiz.q: A Type I error occurs when you:
o: Fail to reject H₀ when H₀ is false
Reject H₀ when H₀ is false
Reject H₀ when H₀ is true
quiz.e: A Type I error is a false alarm: concluding there's an effect when there isn't.

quiz.q: A medical test concludes a patient has a disease they don't have. If H₀ is 'no disease,' this is a:
quiz.e: Rejecting the true null ('no disease') is a Type I error.

quiz.q: Which change increases the power of a test?
quiz.e: More data makes it easier to detect a real effect.

quiz.q: If α = 0.05, what is the probability of a Type I error when H₀ is true?
quiz.e: α is exactly the probability of rejecting H₀ when it's true.

quiz.q: A study of 1,000,000 people finds a new diet lowers weight by 0.1 kg, with P < 0.001. The best conclusion is:
o: The result is statistically significant but probably not practically important
The result must be a Type I error
quiz.e: Huge samples detect tiny effects; significance doesn't mean the effect matters in practice.

quiz.q: A two-sided alternative is appropriate when:
o: You suspect a difference but not its direction
quiz.e: Hₐ: parameter ≠ null value tests for a difference in either direction.

quiz.q: The test statistic z = 2.5 means:
o: The sample result is 2.5 standard errors above the null value
quiz.e: A standardized test statistic measures distance from the null value in standard errors.

quiz.q: Failing to reject H₀ means:
o: The data didn't give convincing evidence against H₀
quiz.e: Absence of evidence isn't proof; H₀ stays plausible.

quiz.q: Power is the probability of:
o: Correctly rejecting H₀ when Hₐ is true
Failing to reject a false H₀
Getting a small P-value when H₀ is true
quiz.e: Power = 1 − P(Type II error).

quiz.q: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 95 instead of 0, comparing values of 96 and 98. The effect is to:
quiz.e: Bars for 96 and 98 would look almost equal from 0; starting at 95 makes one look three times the other.

quiz.q: A headline says a food 'doubles your risk' of a disease, from 1 in 50,000 to 2 in 50,000. The absolute increase is:
quiz.e: The relative increase is 100%, but the absolute increase is tiny: 1 per 50,000.

quiz.q: Unemployment rises from 4% to 6%. Which statement is accurate?
o: It rose 2 percentage points, a 50% relative increase
quiz.e: 6 − 4 = 2 percentage points; 2/4 = 50% relative increase.

quiz.q: A pictograph doubles both the height and width of a money-bag icon to show that savings doubled. Why is this misleading?
o: Money can't be shown with pictures
The area quadruples, exaggerating the change
quiz.e: Scaling both dimensions multiplies the area by 4, so the eye sees a fourfold increase.

quiz.q: Studying only famous college dropouts who became billionaires to conclude that dropping out leads to success is an example of:
quiz.e: The many dropouts who didn't become billionaires are invisible in that sample.

quiz.q: Treatment A has a higher success rate than B at each of two hospitals, but a lower rate when the hospitals are combined. This is:
quiz.e: A lurking variable, such as case severity differing by hospital, reverses the combined trend.

quiz.q: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test is 99% accurate for both sick and healthy people. Among positive results, most are:
quiz.e: Per 100,000 people: about 99 true positives vs. about 999 false positives from the healthy majority.

quiz.q: A company-funded study finds its own product works best. The main concern is:
quiz.e: A source with a stake in the outcome deserves extra scrutiny of methods and reporting.

quiz.q: A graph of a stock shows only the last 3 days, during which it rose. This risks:
quiz.e: A short, chosen window can hide a long-term decline.

quiz.q: A town's mean household income is $250,000 but the median is $48,000. The most likely reason is:
o: A few extremely high incomes skew the mean
quiz.e: Right skew pulls the mean far above the typical (median) household.

quiz.q: An ad says '4 out of 5 dentists recommend' a toothpaste. The most useful follow-up question is:
o: How were the dentists chosen and what exactly were they asked?
quiz.e: Selection and wording determine whether the statistic means anything.

quiz.q: Which claim is best supported by an observational study that finds people who own dogs live longer?
o: Getting a dog will make you live longer
Dogs cause lower blood pressure in everyone
Dog ownership is associated with longer life
quiz.e: Observational data show association; confounders (e.g. activity level, income) could explain it.

flashcards.d: Places each individual into a group or category (e.g. blood type). Summarize with counts or percents.
A numerical value where arithmetic makes sense (e.g. weight in kg).
Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread: the four things to describe about a quantitative distribution, in context.
Long tail toward larger values; mean is usually pulled above the median.
The middle value of ordered data (average of the two middle values if n is even). Resistant to outliers.
Q3 − Q1; the spread of the middle half of the data. Resistant to outliers.
A value is an outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR.
Roughly the typical distance of data values from the mean. Not resistant.
Symmetric, bell-shaped density curve fully described by mean μ and standard deviation σ.
In normal data: ~68% within 1σ, ~95% within 2σ, ~99.7% within 3σ of the mean.
z = (x − μ)/σ; the number of standard deviations a value is from the mean.
The percent of observations at or below a given value.
A curve on or above the axis with total area 1; area over an interval = proportion of observations.
The normal distribution with mean 0 and SD 1; the distribution of z-scores.
Where a normal curve changes concavity; located at μ ± σ.
Calculator function giving the area (proportion) under a normal curve between two bounds.
Graph of two quantitative variables on the same individuals; explanatory on x, response on y.
Measures direction and strength of a linear relationship; between −1 and 1, no units.
Coefficient of determination: fraction of the variation in y explained by the linear model.
A lurking variable related to both explanatory and response, making cause unclear.
Observed y − predicted y; the vertical distance from a point to the regression line.
Using a model to predict far outside the range of the data. Unreliable.
The line minimizing the sum of squared residuals; passes through (x̄, ȳ).
A point whose removal markedly changes the slope, intercept or correlation.
Population: everyone of interest. Sample: the subset actually studied.
Parameter describes a population (μ, p); statistic describes a sample (x̄, p̂).
Every set of n individuals has an equal chance of being chosen.
Divide into similar strata; take an SRS within each stratum.
Divide into clusters; randomly choose whole clusters and survey everyone in them.
When the effects of two variables on the response can't be separated.
Using chance to place subjects into treatment groups; allows causal conclusions.
Improvement caused by believing you received treatment, even a fake one.
The long-run relative frequency of an outcome; a number from 0 to 1.
The set of all possible outcomes of a chance process.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Events that can't happen at the same time; P(A and B) = 0.
One occurring doesn't change the probability of the other; P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B): the chance of A given that B occurred.
Over many trials, the observed proportion approaches the true probability.
The distribution of a statistic's values over all possible samples of the same size.
For large n, the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately normal, regardless of population shape.
Estimated standard deviation of a statistic, e.g. s/√n or √(p̂(1−p̂)/n).
statistic ± margin of error; a range of plausible values for a parameter.
critical value × standard error; accounts for random sampling variation only.
Long-run percent of intervals from the method that capture the true parameter.
n·p̂ ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10, so p̂ is approximately normal.
The claim of no effect or no difference, stated about a parameter.
The claim we seek evidence for: >, < (one-sided) or ≠ (two-sided).
Probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.
Cutoff for 'unusual'; reject H₀ if P-value ≤ α. Equals P(Type I error).
Rejecting H₀ when it's actually true (false positive).
Failing to reject H₀ when Hₐ is true (false negative).
Probability of correctly rejecting a false H₀; 1 − P(Type II).
(statistic − null value)/standard error.
A y-axis that doesn't start at 0, exaggerating differences in bar charts.
Relative: percent change in risk. Absolute: actual change in cases per population.
The arithmetic difference between two percentages (4% → 6% is +2 points).
Drawing conclusions only from cases that 'survived' a selection process.
A trend within every group reverses when the groups are combined, due to a lurking variable.
Ignoring how rare a condition is when interpreting a positive test result.
Showing only the data or time window that supports a conclusion.
When a study's source benefits from a particular result.

PART_A.q: Which pair of summary statistics is most appropriate for a strongly skewed distribution?
PART_A.e: Both median and IQR are resistant to the long tail.

PART_A.q: A data set's five-number summary is 10, 18, 25, 31, 60. Is 60 an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule?
o: No, it is within the range
PART_A.e: IQR = 31 − 18 = 13; the upper fence is 31 + 19.5 = 50.5, and 60 exceeds it.

PART_A.q: Heights of women are approximately normal with mean 64 in and SD 2.5 in. About what percent are taller than 69 in?
PART_A.e: 69 is 2 SD above the mean; about 2.5% of values lie above μ + 2σ.

PART_A.q: A z-score of −2.0 means the value is:
o: Two standard deviations below the mean
PART_A.e: z is measured in standard deviations from the mean.

PART_A.q: A scatterplot of shoe size vs. reading level for elementary students shows r = 0.7. The best explanation is:
o: Age is a confounding variable affecting both
PART_A.e: Older children have both bigger feet and higher reading levels.

PART_A.q: Which statement about r is correct?
o: r = 0 means no relationship of any kind
r = −0.9 indicates a stronger linear relationship than r = 0.6
r has the same units as y

PART_A.q: To determine whether caffeine improves reaction time, the best design is to:
o: Survey coffee drinkers about their reflexes
Compare reaction times of people who choose energy drinks
Measure one person before and after coffee once
Randomly assign volunteers to caffeine or placebo and compare reaction times
PART_A.e: Random assignment with a placebo control supports a causal conclusion.

PART_A.q: Which sampling method gives every possible group of n individuals an equal chance of selection?
PART_A.e: That equal-chance property is the definition of an SRS.

PART_A.q: P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent. What is P(A and B)?
Three independent coin flips are made. What is P(at least one head)?
A 95% confidence interval for a proportion is (0.42, 0.50). The point estimate and margin of error are:
PART_A.e: The estimate is the midpoint; the margin of error is half the width.

PART_A.q: Which is a valid interpretation of a 90% confidence level?
o: 90% of the sample is inside the interval
There is a 90% chance the sample statistic is correct
In repeated sampling, about 90% of such intervals capture the true parameter
The parameter is in the interval 90% of the time it is measured
PART_A.e: The confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the method.

PART_A.q: A researcher tests H₀: μ = 50 vs. Hₐ: μ > 50 and gets P = 0.003. At α = 0.05, the conclusion is:
o: Reject H₀; there is convincing evidence the mean is greater than 50
PART_A.e: P = 0.003 < 0.05, so the result is statistically significant.

PART_A.q: Lowering α from 0.05 to 0.01 (with everything else the same) will:
o: Decrease the chance of a Type I error and decrease power
Increase the chance of a Type I error
PART_A.e: A stricter cutoff makes false alarms rarer but real effects harder to detect.

PART_A.q: A report says crime 'soared 200%' in a small town, from 1 incident to 3. The most accurate response is:
o: Crime in the town has become extremely common
The relative change is large, but the absolute change is only 2 incidents
PART_A.e: With small counts, percent changes can be dramatic while the absolute change is tiny.

PART_A.q: In which situation is Simpson's paradox most likely?
o: Taking a very large random sample
Combining groups that differ in a lurking variable, like case severity
PART_A.e: Uneven distribution of a lurking variable across groups can reverse aggregated trends.

PART_B1.q: Converting temperatures from °C to °F (F = 1.8C + 32) changes the standard deviation by:
PART_B1.e: Adding a constant doesn't affect spread; multiplying by 1.8 does.

PART_B1.q: Which distribution is most likely approximately normal?
o: Heights of adult men in a large country
Wait times at a doctor's office
PART_B1.e: Incomes, pet counts and wait times are typically right-skewed.

PART_B1.q: Removing an outlier that lies far from an otherwise strong linear pattern will usually:
PART_B1.e: The outlier weakens the linear pattern; removing it strengthens the correlation.

PART_B1.q: An experiment on a new teaching method finds improved scores, but students knew they were in the new program and tried harder. This is a concern about:
PART_B1.e: Knowing their group changed the subjects' behavior; blinding would prevent it.

PART_B1.q: In a class, 60% own a phone and 30% own a phone and a tablet. What is P(tablet | phone)?
A researcher wants a 95% margin of error of about 3 percentage points for a proportion near 0.5. Roughly what sample size is needed?
A two-sided 5% significance test rejects H₀: μ = 20. Which 95% confidence interval is consistent with this?
PART_B1.e: Rejecting μ = 20 at α = 0.05 (two-sided) means 20 isn't in the matching 95% interval.

PART_B1.q: Which graph choice gives the most honest comparison of four categories' totals?
o: A bar chart with a y-axis starting at 0
A bar chart with a truncated axis
PART_B1.e: Bars starting at zero keep lengths proportional to the values.

PART_B2.q: Describe what the median and IQR tell you that the mean and standard deviation might not, and give an example of data where this matters.
PART_B2.sa: The median and IQR are resistant, so they describe the typical value and spread of the middle half even when there are outliers or skew. Example: home prices in a town with a few mansions. The mean price and SD are pulled up by the mansions, while the median and IQR still describe a typical home.

PART_B2.q: A study finds students who eat breakfast have higher grades. Explain why this doesn't show breakfast causes higher grades, and name a possible confounding variable.
PART_B2.sa: It is an observational study, so the groups weren't created by random assignment and may differ in other ways. A confounder such as family income or overall sleep and routine could lead to both eating breakfast and higher grades. Only a randomized experiment could show causation.

PART_B2.q: Interpret this result: 'A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of teens who use social media daily is 0.78 to 0.86.'
PART_B2.sa: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.78 to 0.86 captures the true proportion of all teens (in the population sampled) who use social media daily. '95% confident' means the method captures the true proportion in about 95% of repeated samples.

PART_B2.q: In a test of H₀: 'a new drug is no better than the old one', describe a Type I and a Type II error in context, and say which is worse for patients.
PART_B2.sa: Type I: concluding the new drug is better when it isn't, so patients may switch to a drug with no added benefit (and possible side effects or cost). Type II: concluding there's no evidence it is better when it really is, so patients miss out on a better treatment. Which is worse depends on side effects and cost, but a strong answer argues one with a reason.

PART_C.q: Design an experiment to test whether listening to music while studying affects vocabulary quiz scores for 60 volunteer students. Describe treatments, how you'd assign them, what you'd measure, and one way to reduce variability.
PART_C.sa: Treatments: studying the same 30-word list for 20 minutes with music vs. in silence. Assign by numbering students 1–60 and using a random number generator to put 30 in each group (random assignment). Keep other conditions the same (same room, time, word list, quiz). Measure scores on the same vocabulary quiz afterward and compare mean scores. To reduce variability, block by prior vocabulary level (e.g. a pretest), randomizing within each block. Because volunteers were used, results generalize only to similar students, but random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion for them.

PART_C.q: A school claims 70% of its graduates attend college. In a random sample of 200 graduates, 126 attend college (p̂ = 0.63). Carry out a significance test at α = 0.05 of whether the true proportion is less than 0.70.
PART_C.sa: H₀: p = 0.70; Hₐ: p < 0.70, where p is the true proportion of graduates who attend college. Conditions: random sample; 200 is less than 10% of all graduates; np₀ = 140 and n(1 − p₀) = 60 are both at least 10. Test statistic: z = (0.63 − 0.70)/√(0.70·0.30/200) = −0.07/0.0324 ≈ −2.16. P-value = P(Z ≤ −2.16) ≈ 0.015. Since 0.015 < 0.05, reject H₀: there is convincing evidence that fewer than 70% of the school's graduates attend college.
